newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Ireland's Cardinal Daly steps down at 79.
newsitem.headline: Ireland's Cardinal Daly steps down at 79.

text.p: Cardinal Cahal Daly, spiritual head of Ireland's four million Roman Catholics, stepped down as Primate of All Ireland and Archbishop of Armagh on Tuesday, his 79th birthday.

Daly, who succeeded the late Cardinal Tomas O'Fiaich in 1990, was the oldest prelate for 170 years to hold the post of Primate of All Ireland, which covers both the Irish Republic and British-ruled Northern Ireland.
The Irish Republic is more than 90 percent Catholic while in the North Protestants outnumber Catholics three to two.
A philosopher by training, Daly steered the church through a turbulent period in Northern Ireland's history and a series of sexual scandals which tarnished its reputation in the Irish Republic.

In a statement announcing his retirement, Daly said he left the church full of strength and hope despite its recent painful experiences in Ireland. "This is not an end time but a time of new beginning," he said.
Well-known for his forthright condemnation of Irish Republican Army (IRA) violence, Daly warmly welcomed the IRA's 1994 ceasefire only to see it collapse in February this year.

Previously the bishop of Down and Connor for eight years, he had effectively been spiritual head of Belfast's Catholics. He was in the frontline of Northern Ireland's political and sectarian conflict.

His blistering attacks on the IRA prompted some of his flock to walk out of churches but he won praise for bringing job creation schemes to the Belfast slums and getting the security forces to ease up on the police presence at IRA funerals.
A committed ecumenist, Daly was especially preoccupied with the need for peace, reconciliation and mutual acceptance by Protestants and Catholics in Northern Ireland's divided society.
Archbishop Robin Eames, Daly's Protestant counterpart, said he consistently represented the views of his church and people while endeavouring to understand the needs of other traditions.
Daly's final years were marred by a series of sexual scandals involving members of the clergy which undermined the Catholic Church's standing in Ireland.
The disappearance of the Bishop of Galway, Eamonn Casey, in 1992 and later revelations that he had a teenage son proved the first of a series of blows to the church.

Daly then had to deal with a series of child sex abuse scandals, the most serious of which was the jailing of 68-year-old Norbertine priest Brendan Smyth in 1994 after he pleaded guilty to 17 charges of child sex abuse in Northern Ireland.

In a fast modernising Ireland, Daly also faced growing unrest over the issue of clerical celibacy and saw the church's position defeated when a slim majority of Irish people voted to introduce divorce in a referendum last year.

Born in Loughguile, County Antrim, on October 1, 1917, Daly was educated in Belfast, Maynooth, and Paris, and taught classics at St Malachy's College, Belfast, before lecturing in scholastic philosophy at the city's Queen's University.
He was Bishop of Ardagh and Clonmacnois from 1967 to 1982, when he was appointed bishop of Down and Connor.
Daly will be succeeded by Sean Brady, who has been assisting the cardinal since he was appointed coadjutor (archbishop in waiting) in December 1994.
